newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen paying price to ensure grain harvest.
newsitem.headline: China seen paying price to ensure grain harvest.

text.p: China must pay the price of ensuring that its farmers produce enough grain to feed the nation's 1.2 billion people, even if it means heavy subsidies, an agriculture official said on Wednesday.
"Seventy percent of our population is on the farms so we have to protect our farmers," said Zhang Xinmin, an agricultural official with the State Statistical Bureau.
"It doesn't matter if we buy grain (from farmers) above the market price," he told reporters. "We have to protect the interests of farmers."
China's top economic planners huddled last week to draft policies to ensure that farmers were paid adequate prices for their grain as the summer crop was harvested.
The nation's communist rulers want to avoid any unrest among its hundreds of millions of farmers.
Vice Premier Zhu Rongji called on local officials to buy grain at attractive prices to ensure that farmers grew sufficient wheat, rice and corn, even though the nation's grain silos were overflowing.
The top economic policymaker said grain reserves were at record levels, although he did not reveal a figure, which is a state secret.
China expects to report its third consecutive bumper summer harvest this year with the current crop forecast at 115 million tonnes of grain.
The total grain harvest for the year is officially forecast at above 484 million tonnes, down somewhat from the record 490 million tonnes of 1996, partly as a result of less favourable weather.
Government officials, faced with a shortage of funds and no place to store grain, have tried to delay purchases or buy at market prices, which have fallen below state set levels.
Zhang estimated the market price for wheat in some areas of the nation's heartland, the major growing regions of Henan and Anhui, had fallen about 15 percent below the state price.
He declined to say how much the subsidies would cost the government this year but the burden would have to be borne.
Beijing has pleaded with farmers to help the government with its grain storage headaches, asking them to keep some stockpiles on the farm.
It has tried to assure them there is no need to sell all of their crop now because grain will fetch an equal price in future.
"Farmers should not rush to sell their grain," said Zhang.
The official turned aside arguments by many economists who insist that China can afford to grow less grain and should encourage its farmers to raise other more valuable cash crops.
But self-sufficiency in grain has become a mantra for China's Communist Party leaders who recall only too clearly the famine that killed tens of millions of people less than four decades ago.
"China should mainly rely on itself to feed its population," said Zhang.
"If it relies on the international market, that would become a burden for the Chinese government and would affect the world market."
